words.prose: {{ar:مِنَ}} ({{tr:mina}}) opens the ayah as a dependent source phrase, not as a fresh independent sentence. It governs {{ar:ٱللَّهِ}} ({{tr:allāhi}}), so the punishment already asked for and declared unrepellable in 70:1-2 receives its origin here. The particle is therefore not partitive or merely explanatory; it marks the punishment as from God and, in this context, causally grounded in that source. Its fixed unrooted shape still carries real grammatical weight: a small function word supplies the genitive dependency, while its final vowel and nasal onset keep the source phrase moving audibly into the divine name. That makes the ayah boundary itself feel like continuation before the epithet expands the source.

words.prose: {{ar:ٱللَّهِ}} ({{tr:allāhi}}) is the governed complement of {{ar:مِنَ}} ({{tr:mina}}), so the name fills the source slot while remaining grammatically dependent. The form is the definite proper divine name, not an ordinary class noun, and this makes the punishment-source relation personal and authoritative. The wider root discussion around worship, refuge, bewilderment, and awe survives as pressure around the scene: protection from the punishment has just been denied, and the source is the very one before whom refuge and awe converge. The name also pivots into {{ar:ذِي ٱلْمَعَارِجِ}} ({{tr:dhī l-maʿāriji}}), turning source attribution into a title-like epithet; the familiar divine name receives the rare ascent-domain attribute, and 70:4 then shows that domain in motion. Recitationally, the liaison after the preposition and the repeated genitive i-cadence make source, possessor, and possessed domain sound like one descending chain.

words.prose: {{ar:ذِي}} ({{tr:dhī}}) is the hinge of the epithet. Its genitive five-noun form agrees with the governed environment around {{ar:ٱللَّهِ}} ({{tr:allāhi}}), while its construct shape points forward to {{ar:ٱلْمَعَارِجِ}} ({{tr:al-maʿāriji}}). That makes possession or characterization unavoidable: the ascent domain is not an unattached image but the attribute by which the divine source is named here. The broader root has relative, demonstrative, and interrogative branches, yet the local form selects the possessor-title branch; the phrase feels formulaic like other possessor epithets while remaining singular in its ascent content. The long genitive vowel of the five-noun form also participates in the repeated i-cadence, so the same word acts as grammatical joint, title-maker, and sound-link.

words.prose: {{ar:ٱلْمَعَارِجِ}} ({{tr:al-maʿāriji}}) completes the epithet as the governed complement of {{ar:ذِي}} ({{tr:dhī}}). Its definiteness and plural form make the domain sound like an established multiplicity of ascent routes, not one newly introduced ladder or a bare abstraction of elevation. The noun keeps concrete route-infrastructure in view while allowing rank-like hierarchy: the image is a traversable vertical system under divine possession. Wider root-family pressures of limping, bending, winding, and causing ascent are narrowed by the local form, but they sharpen the idea of ascent as staged, path-dependent movement. The word is rare as a concrete noun and contrastively appears in a worldly luxury setting (43:33); here it becomes a divine-cosmological attribute. By closing 70:3, it also opens 70:4, where the same root becomes enacted ascent. Its final genitive cadence closes the chain, while the root's movement from deep throat through liquid to palatal closure gives the ascent noun an audible rising arc.

baseline_models.mechanism: The worshipped one is named as possessor of multiple ways of upward movement, so vertical access is presented as an owned domain rather than as free space or a single ladder.

changed_reading.before: Min Allah is an isolated statement of origin and ma'arij is a separate majestic title.

summary.what_was_special: The plural ma'arij supported several coexisting mechanisms: governed traffic, changing scale, nonmaterial architecture, practiced stations, horizon cycles, and a closing vertical reversal. Split-root and interval images also yielded contained outliers without replacing the ordinary ascent sense.
remaining_uncertainties: Waqi' may express inevitable occurrence rather than literal falling, which would weaken the bidirectional spatial model but not the provenance model.
The ethical sequence and the plural horizon title may resonate with ma'arij without intentionally explaining it.
Curving, stopping, extracted-path, and cadence images are root-level activations whose lexical force in ma'arij remains exploratory.

reader_a.activated_readings_md:
1. **Authority is pictured as a structured route of ascent.** The plural *maʿārij* anchors **ع ر ج, B004, “ascent upward,”** whose scope includes a way or device of ascent. The immediate repetition as a verb in 70:4 turns the divine epithet into functioning spatial infrastructure, while the final rush toward an erected goal (70:43) supplies an inverted human route. I infer that ordered access belongs to God, whereas the condemned merely hurry toward a terminal marker. The ayah reads as naming the possessor of channels that govern approach, not simply “the high.”

2. **The routes need not be imagined as straight.** **ع ر ج, B002, “curving, bending, or turning aside,”** remains visible beside B004, and the packet later emphasizes eastings and westings (70:40), repeated directional turns, and those who turn their backs (70:17). The abductive move is that ascent may require staged or curved traversal rather than direct human measure. This makes the fifty-thousand-year measure in 70:4 a warning against reducing divine approach to a straight human scale.
reader_a.retrospective_surprises_md: The final rush toward a *nuṣub* in 70:43 unexpectedly supplied a downward human counter-route to the ordered *maʿārij*: both are directed paths, but only the first belongs to divine access and measure.

concept_map.definition: Bir varlığa tapınma eylemini ve kişinin kendini tapınmaya vermesini anlatır. Türemiş kullanımlarda bir varlığı tapınılır kılmayı, tapınılan varlığı ve tapınma konusu sayılan varlıkları da adlandırır.
